title: Chanting in Zen
hook: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors

segments.voice: Yesterday: the wooden board, and your line, time passes swiftly. Did a knock or a timer stop you for one breath? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

Zen has a reputation for silence, so the morning service can come as a surprise. Before breakfast, the whole hall stands or kneels and chants, loudly, in one low, steady pitch. A hollow wooden drum, carved in the shape of a fish, keeps the beat: tok, tok, tok. Nobody is performing. Nobody is singing harmony. Voices that don't match blend into one sound that seems to fill the floorboards. Then it stops, and the silence afterward feels different. Today: chanting in Zen.
screen: `A SILENT SCHOOL THAT CHANTS.` → `ONE LOW PITCH, ONE BEAT.` → `THE SILENCE AFTER.`

segments.voice: First, the Heart Sutra. You met it earlier on this path: the short text where Avalokiteshvara sees that all five heaps are empty, and tells Shariputra that form is emptiness and emptiness is form. In Zen halls it's chanted often, in Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese or English, depending on the community. Chanting it isn't the same as studying it. The aim is to let the text pass through the body until it's breath, not argument. Second, the four vows. These are the bodhisattva vows, said together, often at the end of a service. In plain paraphrase: beings are without number, and I vow to free them. Delusions never run out, and I vow to end them. The gates of the teaching are without limit, and I vow to enter them. The Buddha's way is beyond reach, and I vow to embody it. Notice the shape. Each vow names something impossible, and promises it anyway. Third, the names of the ancestors. Some services chant the lineage: the Buddha, then teacher after teacher, down to the founders of that community's line. It's a family tree said aloud, a way of remembering that this practice came hand to hand, through people. Fourth, why chant at all in a school of sitting. Chanting uses the whole body: breath, belly, throat. It's hard to chant at full voice and think about lunch at the same time. And chanting together makes the hall one body, the same way kinhin made it one line. Zen silence and Zen chanting aren't opposites. Both are ways of being entirely here.
screen: `THE HEART SUTRA, AS BREATH.` · `FOUR VOWS, EACH IMPOSSIBLE.` · `THE ANCESTORS, NAME BY NAME.` · `ONE VOICE, ONE BODY.` · then, large: `CHANTING ZEN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Sit up, and take a full breath into the belly. If you practice, you can say the four vows in your community's wording. If not, you can simply say the plain paraphrase from today, slowly, in one low, steady tone: beings are without number, I vow to free them, and so on through all four. Let the voice come from low down. Don't worry about the words being perfect. Feel the sound in your chest. Then sit in the quiet that follows. The bell holds the time.
Chanting in Zen. The Heart Sutra, the four vows and the names of the ancestors, chanted together in one low voice, as practice for the whole body. Today's word.
Your line: chanting zen. Today, when you hum, sing along or say something aloud, let your whole attention be in the sound for that moment. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Zen communities hold chanting services, often morning and evening, where the Heart Sutra, the four bodhisattva vows, dedications and sometimes the names of the lineage ancestors are chanted together in a steady tone, often kept in time by a wooden drum.

fork.setup: you're chanting the four vows: beings are without number, I vow to free them. a voice in you says that's impossible. what does the vow do with that?
options: keeps the vow anyway, knowing it can't be finished.
changes it to a smaller number.
fork.reveal: the vows name the impossible on purpose. they're said anyway, as a direction to walk in, not a task to complete.

original.note: Japanese: shiguseigan, the four great bodhisattva vows chanted in Zen services.

trapdoor: what you thought: Zen is all silence.
what it means: Zen chants too: the Heart Sutra, the four vows, the names of the ancestors, in one low voice.
what a scholar hears: the vows are built on impossibility: each names something endless and vows it anyway.
